title: Germany's Fragile Recovery: Growth Returns, but Costs and Political Risks Cloud the Outlook
excerpt: Germany's government has upgraded its growth forecast for 2026, citing stronger exports and public investment, but persistently high inflation and energy costs are limiting what citizens feel in their daily lives. At the same time, rising support for the far-right Alternative für Deutschland is increasingly framed not only as a political challenge but as a risk to investment and long-term economic stability. The gap between official optimism and lived experience is at the heart of both debates.
body:
A Better Forecast, but a Recovery Still on Paper

The German federal government has raised its 2026 growth forecast from 0.5 percent to 1.3 percent, with 1.1 percent projected for 2027. Officials attribute the improved outlook to stronger export performance, a ramp-up in infrastructure and defence spending, and an economy that has proved more resilient than many analysts expected. The coalition's argument is that sustained public investment can generate employment, attract private capital and restore Germany's standing as Europe's industrial anchor.

The case for optimism is not without foundation. Germany remains the European Union's largest economy, and any durable rebound would have significant knock-on effects for suppliers, manufacturers and labour markets across the continent. If public spending crowds in private investment, the government argues, the current squeeze on households could prove temporary.

However, the headline numbers tell a more complicated story. Inflation is forecast at 2.7 percent in 2026 and 3.0 percent in 2027, meaning that real purchasing power remains under pressure even as gross domestic product rises. Energy prices continue to weigh on both household budgets and production costs for industry. The most accurate characterisation of the current moment is not a recovery fully felt, but growth returning alongside continued cost-of-living strain.

Investor Confidence Slips as Energy Costs Bite

The mood among institutional investors and analysts reflects that ambiguity. The ZEW index of investor expectations fell from 34.7 to 28.1 in October, with analysts citing energy prices as a significant drag on consumption and investment. While the survey showed some improvement in the assessment of current conditions, it identified no clear new momentum in the final months of the year, suggesting that the upgraded growth forecast has not yet translated into decisive confidence among those placing capital.

Trade unions and opposition voices have sharpened that critique. Their argument is that GDP growth does not automatically equal improved welfare for workers. Rising energy bills, concerns about job security in energy-intensive sectors and fears about weakening social protections mean that employees are being asked, in effect, to absorb the costs of industrial transition. For the coalition led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, the political challenge is to make the recovery visible in wages and public services before patience runs out.

The AfD's Rise as a Political and Economic Warning Signal

Parallel to the cost-of-living debate, the growing electoral success of the Alternative für Deutschland is prompting a broader conversation about whether political polarisation has itself become an economic risk. Business leaders have publicly linked the party's gains to concerns about Germany's attractiveness to foreign investors and skilled migrants, arguing that a more unpredictable political environment raises the cost of long-term commitments in the country.

The government's response has been to accelerate its investment and reform agenda, with officials pointing to more than 225 billion euros in pledged investment commitments secured at a Berlin business summit as evidence that political risk has not paralysed capital flows. The pro-government argument is that credible economic delivery is the most effective counter to populist movements: if living standards improve visibly, the appeal of anti-establishment parties should diminish.

The AfD's own argument inverts that logic. The party contends that established parties created the conditions for its rise through high energy costs, weak growth, migration pressures and what it portrays as institutional unresponsiveness. A separate critique from the left warns that mainstream parties risk using the AfD's advance to justify spending cuts and weaker labour protections, when the more effective answer to polarisation would be stronger wages, better public services and targeted investment in regions already hollowed out by industrial change. The defensible conclusion, based on available evidence, is that the AfD represents a growing risk to political predictability and labour-market openness, though the data do not yet support claims that the party has independently caused a measurable collapse in investment.

A Feedback Loop That Could Define the Decade

Taken together, the two debates point toward a feedback loop that policymakers are racing to break. Weak economic confidence, driven partly by energy costs and inflation, is fuelling political anger. That political anger, in turn, makes coalition governance harder, complicates reform, and introduces uncertainty that gives investors pause. If the loop tightens, Germany could find itself in a position where macroeconomic improvement arrives too slowly to arrest social and political deterioration.

The stakes extend beyond Germany's borders. A more polarised Berlin would affect EU-level decisions on migration, fiscal rules, defence spending, industrial strategy and continued support for Ukraine. Germany's traditional partners in the bloc, from France to the Nordic states, are watching closely whether the coalition can demonstrate that democratic governance and economic reform can outpace populist mobilisation.

The next several months will be decisive. Inflation data in early 2026, the pace at which pledged investment commitments translate into actual jobs and output, and the coalition's ability to hold together under sustained pressure will determine whether the gap between official forecasts and everyday experience begins to close. If it does not, the risk is that Germany's recovery remains a statistical phenomenon rather than a political stabiliser, leaving the field open to forces whose prescriptions carry risks of their own.
keywords: Germany, economic recovery, AfD, Alternative für Deutschland, inflation, energy prices, investor confidence, ZEW index, Friedrich Merz, EU economy, political polarisation, cost of living, foreign investment, skilled labour, GDP growth
sources: German Federal Government 2026-2027 growth and inflation forecasts; ZEW Centre for European Economic Research, October investor expectations survey; Berlin Business Summit investment commitment figures
